## Methods

Materials
The phospholipids, 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC), 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC), 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(lissamine rhodamine B sulfonyl) (ammonium salt) (Rho-PE), 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(7-nitro-2-1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-yl) (ammonium salt) (NBD-PE) were purchased from Avanti polar lipids (IL, USA). Hydrochloric acid (CAS: 7647-01-0), sodium hydroxide (CAS: 1310-73-2), polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) (CAS: 9002-89-5), cholesterol (CAS: 57-88-5), adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP) disodium salt hydrate (CAS: 34369-07-8) and poly(acrylic acid sodium salt) [PAA, M = 5,100 g mol-1] (CAS: 9003-04-7), DEAE-dextran hydrochloride [DEAE-dex, M = 500,000 g mol-1] (CAS:9064-91-9) and CM-dextran sodium salt [CM-dex, M = 10,000-20,000 g mol-1] (CAS:39422-83-8) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. PDMS (Sylgard 184) was purchased from Dow Corning. Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) [PDDA, M = 8,500 g mol-1, 28 wt. % in H O] (CAS: 26062-79-3) was purchased from Polysciences. Cyanine 5-labelled single stranded DNA (Cy5-ssDNA) was purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (the sequence is provided in Supplementary Table 1).

Giant vesicle preparation
Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) were prepared by the modified lipid film hydration method as reported elsewhere.43 Briefly, 50 μL of the desired lipid or lipid mixture solution at 4 mM in chloroform were spin coated onto a glass slide at 1,000 rpm for 120 seconds at room temperature. The lipid compositions were as follow: 99.9 mol% DOPC + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE (DOPC), 69.9 mol% DOPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE (DOPC/cholesterol), 99 mol% DPPC + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DPPC), 69 mol% DPPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DPPC/cholesterol), 34.9 mol% DOPC + 34 mol% DPPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol). The spin coated lipid film on the glass slide was dried under vacuum for 1h to remove any traces of chloroform. A rectangular chamber was assembled using a PTFE spacer (25 mm x 35 mm x 5 mm), filled with 500 μL of a 200 mM sucrose solution (swelling solution), and closed with a second glass slide held with two binder clips. The dried lipid film was hydrated with this swelling solution for 30 minutes at 25°C for DOPC and DOPC/cholesterol lipid films and 60°C for DPPC/cholesterol and DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol lipid films using a heating plate equipped with a temperature controller (IKA RCT standard 2.0). The resulting suspension of GUVs was transferred to Eppendorf tubes shielded from light to avoid photobleaching and stored at room temperature for a maximum duration of one week.

Preparation of stock solutions for coacervate formulation
Stock solutions of PDDA, PAA and ATP were prepared at 100 mM or 1 M (expressed in monomer concentrations) by diluting the 28 wt% PDDA solution or dissolving the appropriate amount of PAA or ATP powder using Milli-Q water and adjusting the pH to 8.0 with NaOH (1M) or HCl (1M). The concentration of ATP was checked via UV-Vis spectroscopy (PerkinElmer) at 260 nm using an excitation co-efficient of 15.4 × 103 L mol-1 cm-1. Carboxymethyl (CM)-dextran and diethylaminoethyl (DEAE)-dextran stock solutions were made at 50-100 mg mL-1 in Milli-Q water and the pH adjusted to 8.0. Given that the fraction of charge units on these polysaccharides is not defined, we do not provide a charge concentration for these two polymers but keep the concentration as mg mL-1. All stock solutions were stored at 4°C, expect for ATP where aliquots were stored at -20°C.

Coacervate characterization
Turbidity screening: The optimal polymer ratio for PDDA/PAA coacervate formation was determined by measuring the turbidity at 700 nm of 20 µL solutions prepared at fixed (5 mM) PDDA and variable PAA concentrations (0.5-50 mM) in sucrose/glucose medium (90 mM each, final concentration) using a 384-well plate (Corning, flat bottom) and a microplate spectrophotometer (Molecular Devices). For critical salt concentration (CSC) determination, 20 µL coacervates suspensions were prepared at 10 mM PDDA and 10 mM, 5 mM or 5 mg mL-1 PAA, ATP, CM-dextran, respectively; or 10 mM PAA and 4 mg mL-1 DEAE-dextran in sucrose/glucose medium (90 mM each, final concentration) and varying NaCl concentrations and the turbidity determined at 700 nm. The data was fitted with a sigmoidal logistic function. The CSC was determined by extrapolating the first-order derivative at the inflection point to zero turbidity.

Interfacial tension measurements: The interfacial tension of the different coacervates were estimated by the interfacial profile between the dense coacervate phase and dilute supernatant after macroscopic phase separation in a cell with parallel walls at room temperature, as described in ref. 44. Coacervate suspensions were here prepared at high concentration to produce sufficient amount of bulk coacervate phase, specifically, for PDDA/PAA: 200 mM PDDA and 200 mM PAA; for PDDA/ATP: 60 mM PDDA and 30 mM ATP; for PDDA/CM-dextran: 50 mM PDDA and 25 mg mL-1 CM-dextran; for DEAE-dextran/PAA: 40 mg mL-1 DEAE-dextran and 100 mM PAA. All systems except PDDA/ATP were formulated in sucrose/glucose medium (90 mM each, final concentration). These suspensions were placed into a 1 mm thick quartz cell (Hellma), then centrifuged at 1,400 ×g for 5 minutes to favor complete macroscopic phase separation, resulting in a net interface between a denser polymer-rich (coacervate) phase and a polymer-dilute (supernatant) upper phase. ### Reviewer 1

This manuscript investigates how coacervate droplets interact with lipid membranes of differing fluidity by tuning the
polyelectrolyte charge ratio of PDDA and PAA. The authors demonstrate that coacervates preferentially wet more fluid
(liquid-disordered) membranes and that this wetting behavior is modulated not only by the PDDA/PAA ratio but also by the
chemical nature of the coacervate components. By comparing several types of coacervates, the study highlights the
selective wetting phenomenon as a generalizable feature, potentially governed by the viscosity of the
coacervate and the properties of the membrane phase. This manuscript presents potentially publishable results; however, the current version
lacks sufficient statistical robustness, mechanistic depth, and accurate contextual framing (e.g., in terms of relevance to
origins-of-life). Substantial additional discussion, quantitative analysis, and clarification are needed before the manuscript
can be reconsidered for publication.
1) Although the study conceptually addresses the origin of life in the Introduction, the use of synthetic polymers (PDDA and
PAA), which lack direct biological relevance, may weaken the argument. The manuscript appears to overstate the
significance of the system to prebiotic chemistry, and I suggest the authors moderate their claims regarding the implications
for origins-of-life research.
2) The observation that zeta potential becomes significantly negative upon the addition of only 0.1–1 mol% of fluorescent
lipids is puzzling, especially considering the use of a neutral sucrose buffer. The authors should clarify the mechanism
underlying this drastic shift and explain whether such small additions can indeed induce meaningful surface charge
changes.
3) The dataset for quantifying wetting interactions (n = 5) appears limited. Additionally, the authors themselves acknowledge
that deformation length ratio (L*) is size-dependent. It would strengthen the study to include the vesicle/coacervate size
ratios for each condition and present trends of φ and L* as a function of this size ratio to ensure meaningful comparison.
4) In the main text (page 5), what is referred to as "Figure 2a(ii)" appears to be a mislabeling and should be "Figure 2d(ii)".
5) The finding that membrane fluidity (rather than charge) dominates wetting behavior is highly interesting. However, the
discussion of the underlying physicochemical mechanism is insufficient. Since membrane adhesion typically results from a
balance between attractive and repulsive forces, I suggest the authors discuss—preferably quantitatively—how vesicle
membrane fluidity (i.e., deformability) and coacervate viscosity contribute to the overall adhesion energy. Why does
complete fusion not occur among the tested conditions? Is there an inherent incompatibility in material properties between
the coacervates and vesicles?
6) It would be helpful to include representative images used to calculate the interfacial tension and to indicate which
parameters (x, y, h, and so on) correspond to the length in the image.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Joseph et al. describes the interaction between coacervates and GUV membranes composed of either
ordered or disordered liquid lipid phases. This significant manuscript is, in my opinion, highly relevant to a broad audience,
including researchers in origin-of-life studies and materials science. However, I have several concerns that should be
addressed through discussion or additional experiments:
Does temperature influence the wetting behavior? Investigating temperature’s role in wetting behavior is crucial, as it often
influences molecular interactions and phase behavior in lipid systems.
The manuscript lacks mechanistic discussion, particularly regarding the molecular interactions driving selective wetting. The
lack of mechanistic discussion is a significant gap in many studies of complex systems like coacervates and GUVs.
Although computational modelling is out-of-scope, I would encourage a thorough discussion to clarify this.
Is the wetting behavior permanent or reversible over time? Does it evolve or change in morphology? Time-lapse imaging
could clarify this.
The authors draw parallels to living cells, but these comparisons are vague, as the systems are synthetic and engineered.
Could these systems be adapted for use with living systems? How might one engineer systems exhibiting similar behavior
in biological contexts? By using biologically relevant electrolytes for instance?This is, in my opinion, critical for broader
applications. For example, could biologically relevant polyelectrolytes be used?

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript describes how coacervate droplets contact lipid membranes as a function of the lipid ordering in the
membrane (liquid disordered DOPC and DOPC/cholesterol vs liquid ordered DPPC and DPPC/cholesterol membranes)
and shows preferential wetting of lipid membrane domains by coacervates that depend on coacervate composition. The
authors have examined multiple coacervate compositions and demonstrated that the most obvious explanations based on
charge-charge interactions alone cannot explain their results for these systems, in which the membranes are based on
zwitterionic lipids. They have quantified wetting behavior from image analysis to compare multiple
coacervate-membrane combinations and provide measurements on the coacervate physical properties such as surface charge,
interfacial tension and viscosity. Although a compelling overall explanation for the findings is not clear, the authors have shown that a variety of
outcomes can be achieved based on the combination of coacervate composition and membrane phase (Lo vs Ld), and that
coacervates can preferentially interact with only one membrane phase domain in mixed-phase membranes. The work will
interest the large and growing community of researchers interested in coacervate-lipid membrane contact and wetting, which
is increasingly understood to play crucial roles in cell biology and is further of interest for design of artificial cells and
potential relevance to the origins of life.
I do have some comments and suggestions for improving the manuscript:
1. The discussion is somewhat lacking in explanations for the observed results and would benefit from some additional
content. For example, the authors point to coacervate viscosity as a key determinant of the coacervate-membrane
interactions, but do not provide a mechanism by which coacervate viscosity would have this effect. Additionally, the authors
found that coacervate surface tensions were not predictive, and I wonder if considering all relevant surface tensions
(coacervate-dilute phase, coacervate-membrane, and membrane-dilute phase) would be more instructive, particularly since
free polyelectrolytes from the coacervate suspension are likely to be interacting with the membranes (see also next
comment). The discussion of ATP-membrane interactions and their potential role is interesting and raises the broader
question of how all the coacervate molecules interact with the membranes to potentially change their properties.
2. The coacervate suspensions added to the vesicle samples also bring with them molecules in the dilute phase, that could
interact with lipid membranes even if the coacervates do not contact the membranes. This possibility is not discussed in the
manuscript but could in principle play an important role in the outcomes, particularly for any experiments where the relative

3. Characterization of the physical properties of the coacervates do not appear to have been performed in the same medium
as the membrane interaction experiments. Coacervate surface tension and viscosity is likely different in their initial
suspensions, which contain the coacervate and dilute phases, than after addition to the vesicle samples, which contain a
substantial concentration of sugars (sucrose/glucose) from the vesicle preparation. What impact does this have on
coacervate properties?
4. Why are the membranes charged (Figure 2b)? DOPC and DPPC are both zwitterionic, and both have the same
headgroup. Is the relatively large negative zeta potential for DOPC membranes, and the positive zeta potential for DPPC
membranes expected from prior literature?
5. The manuscript does not mention earlier LLPS-membrane studies that used PEG/dextran LLPS. This is a missed
opportunity to compare/contrast these new findings with the prior work (see, for example, an overview in Annu. Rev.
Biophys. 2024. 53:319–41, and specific examples that also incorporate Lo/Ld domains in the phase-contacting lipid
membranes: Nature Chem. 2024. 16: 54–62, Am. Chem. Soc. 2008. 130(23): 7400–7406). The current manuscript’s work is

model system for most aspects of biocondensates than the PEG/dextran ATPS and which can be expected to have more
varied membrane wetting properties than PEG/dextran systems.
6. The SI notes that 10 minutes elapsed after mixing before imaging. Did the wetting behavior change further over time or did
it remain constant after 10 minutes?
7. In the SI, the authors state how the “Selective wetting quantification” was performed. I found the explanation confusing as
it seemed that several types of potentially important wetting scenarios were excluded from analysis (“wetting on both
membrane domains” and “complete wetting” were excluded). This requires further explanation, since it would seem
important to include these events in datasets meant to elucidate selective wetting behavior.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as a key biological paradigm, playing a critical role in cellular compartmentalization and potentially contributing to the origins of life. Lipid membranes are equally important in these processes, serving as selective barriers that define and protect cellular environments. Recent studies have revealed a dynamic interaction between LLPS and lipid membranes, both in cellulo and in biomimetic systems. In vitro studies typically use simplified model membranes, while biological membranes are far more complex, often exhibiting phase-separated domains. Despite growing interest, the relationship between lipid phase separation within membranes and LLPS remains largely unexplored. Here, we explore how coacervates interact with membranes composed of liquid-ordered or liquid-disordered lipid phases using giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). We show that coacervate-membrane interactions are modulated by coacervate composition and lipid domain properties. Notably, we report the selective wetting of lipid domains in phase separated GUVs. Different coacervates exhibit distinct wetting behaviors, with variations in their composition influencing whether they preferentially wet liquid-disordered or liquid-ordered lipid domains, highlighting the coacervate-specific nature of these interactions. These findings highlight how lipid phase separation can mediate selective membrane wetting, offering insights into condensate-membrane interactions in cells and in simplified cell-like model systems.

---

## Introduction

Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is emerging as a central paradigm in biology,1 and is hypothesized to have played a role in the emergence of protocells.2 In living cells, phase-separated droplets, known as biomolecular condensates, perform critical biological functions, such as metabolic regulation, signal transduction and stress management.3 In vitro, droplets produced by associative LLPS between polymers or surfactants, known as coacervates, capture key physicochemical properties of biomolecular condensates,4 5 including increased viscosity and reduced surface tension, but also serve as plausible protocell models by concentrating chemical species,6 7 enabling reactions that would otherwise be unfavorable in aqueous environments.8-11

Lipid membranes are also fundamental to both cellular and protocellular compartmentalization and evolution.1 Modern cells, but also a number of intracellular organelles, are delineated by complex proteolipidic membranes that form selectively permeable barriers capable of regulating the exchange of solutes. This structural role is equally important when considering the origins of life, as simple membranes must have been essential to define and separate the internal protocell environment from the surrounding medium.14

These two forms of compartmentalization – phase-separated droplets and membrane-bounded structures – are not mutually exclusive. Recent studies have highlighted the interactions between liquid-liquid phase separation and lipid membranes, revealing a dynamic interplay that influences both cellular function and protocell models. In living cells, biomolecular condensates often interact closely with lipid membranes.15 These interactions can drive processes such as membrane remodeling16 and protein recruitment,17 playing a key role in cellular dynamics and signaling pathways. In vitro, early experimental studies using PEG/dextran aqueous two-phase systems (ATPS) encapsulated within giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) provided foundational insights into membrane wetting and the role of interfacial tension balance in determining wetting morphology.18 19 More recent studies have delved deeper into the mechanisms by which coacervates interact with lipid membranes.19-21 On the one hand, the interfacial assembly of lipids around coacervates creates hybrid protocells, combining a crowded interior able to accumulate chemicals with a physical barrier that prevents droplet coalescence and limits material exchange.22-25 On the other hand, pioneering studies have started investigating interactions between biomolecular condensates or coacervates and model lipid membranes using GUVs. In a seminal example, electrostatic interactions and hydrophobic lipid bilayer anchoring were shown to promote coacervate binding to membranes.26 More recently, charge-dependent wetting of GUVs by coacervates was reported to modulate lipid packing27 and induce membrane remodeling,28 with examples showing that strong coacervate-vesicle interactions favored partial or complete endocytosis of the droplets within the GUVs.29 30

These observations represent the first steps towards elucidating coacervate-membrane interactions based on non-specific interactions. However, cellular membranes are composed of complex lipid mixtures, where lipid phase separation can give rise to domains enriched in specific lipid species. This complexity, driven by the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of biological membranes, raises fundamental questions about the role of lipid composition, membrane fluidity and domain formation in modulating coacervate-membrane interactions. In this context, the interplay between lipid phase separation within bilayers and liquid-liquid phase separation remains largely unexplored. Recent work has shown a dynamic interplay between domain formation in ternary lipid membranes and LLPS using PEG/dextran systems.31 In parallel, a study revealed that condensates preferentially interact with liquid-disordered domains in phase-separated membranes, highlighting the need to understand how both lipid composition and the chemical nature of the condensate control this selectivity.32

Here, we assemble GUVs using high- and low-melting temperature lipids, forming either liquid-disordered or liquid-ordered bilayers. We investigate their interactions with polyelectrolyte-based coacervates prepared at varying positive-to-negative charge ratios. We find that electrostatic interactions are not the primary driver of coacervate-vesicle interactions; rather, the lipid composition dictates the preferential affinity of coacervates for more fluid membranes. We identify conditions where coacervates selectively wet one type of GUVs in a binary vesicle population. Additionally, using phase-separated vesicles with micron-sized lipid domains, we demonstrate that coacervates selectively wet fluid domains, irrespective of net surface charges. We further demonstrate that such wetting is reversibly modulated by temperature, reflecting changes in lipid mixing. Importantly, we find that selective domain wetting can be inverted depending on the chemical nature of the coacervate, revealing that coacervate chemistry provides an additional lever, complementary to membrane composition, for tuning membrane affinity. Altogether, these insights underscore the potential of lipid phase separation to mediate selective membrane wetting by coacervates, offering a compelling framework for understanding the role of condensate-membrane interactions in cells and in simplified cell-like model systems.

---

## Results

Surface charge does not dictate selective coacervate-membrane interactions
Our model coacervate droplets were assembled by mixing poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDDA, M = 8,300 g mol-1, 5-20 mM expressed in charge concentration) and poly(sodium acrylate) (PAA, M = 5,100 g mol-1) close to charge stoichiometry in water at pH 8 (Figure 1a). Optical microscopy images of the obtained turbid suspension confirmed the formation of liquid-like micrometer-sized coacervate droplets (Figure 1b). Turbidity screening revealed that optimal coacervation conditions were met at charge neutrality, although some turbidity persisted for a PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio comprised between 0.6 and 2 (Supplementary Figure 1). The coacervate surface charge changed from negative to positive by tuning the polyelectrolyte charge ratio within this range (Figure 2a). Coacervate droplets were fluorescently labeled by spontaneous sequestration of Cyanine 5-tagged single-stranded DNA (Cy5-ssDNA, 10 µM, Supplementary Table 1) (Figure 1b, inset).

Model giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) were prepared using the lipid film hydration method in a 200 mM sucrose buffer, first employing either DOPC (T = -20 °C) or DPPC (T = +41.3 °C). Due to their low melting temperature, DOPC phospholipids formed membranes in a liquid disordered phase at room temperature33 34 (ℓ , Figure 1c). In contrast, the high rigidity of DPPC membranes at room temperature (gel phase33) hindered proper GUV formation, even when lipid film hydration was performed at 60°C (Supplementary Figure 2). To address this, 30 mol% cholesterol was added during DPPC lipid film formation to increase membrane fluidity and produce a liquid-ordered lipid phase35 36 (ℓ , Figure 1d), allowing for a higher GUV production yield. The DOPC- and DPPC-based GUVs were labelled with red fluorescent (Rho-PE, 0.1 mol%, Figure 1e, coloring to magenta was used) and green fluorescent (NBD-PE, 1 mol%, Figure 1f) lipids, respectively. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching confirmed the higher lateral mobility of the lipids within DOPC membranes compared to DPPC ones (Figure 2c). Both types of vesicles exhibited a negative net charge (Figure 2b), in line with previous reports,37 38 with a slightly less negative ζ-potential observed in DPPC GUVs likely due to the addition of the fluorescently labelled NBD-PE lipid (Supplementary Figure 3).

We next mixed GUVs and coacervates in an imaging chamber to investigate their interactions using confocal fluorescence microscopy. We noted that a small fraction (approx. 20%) of the GUVs broke during this mixing step, possibly due to osmotic stress or shearing by pipetting. Nevertheless, a sufficient fraction of GUVs remained intact and was used to characterize interactions with coacervates. As an example, coacervates prepared at a PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio of 0.7 (negative surface charge) appeared to partially wet DOPC vesicles (Figure 1g) but did not interact with DPPC/cholesterol vesicles (Figure 1h). Since both types of GUVs carried a net negative ζ-potential (Figure 2b), these preliminary observations suggested that differences in electrostatic attraction could not account for the selective interaction of coacervates with DOPC vesicles.

To test this hypothesis further, we then systematically varied the PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio, thereby altering the net surface charge of the coacervates (Figure 2a), and monitored their interactions with GUVs. We found that coacervates prepared with a large excess of PAA (8 mM; ζ < 0 mV) did not interact with any of the GUVs (ζ < 0 mV), as indicated by the coexistence of non-adhering and non-deformed droplets and vesicles (Figure 2d(i,iii)). This suggested that electrostatic repulsion between same-charge coacervates and GUVs suppressed adhesion. In contrast, coacervates prepared at equimolar or lower amounts of PAA (≤ 5 mM; ζ > 0 mV) interacted with both types of GUVs (ζ < 0 mV), consistent with electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged compartments. Under these conditions, we only observed partial wetting, which primarily caused deformations to the lipid membranes while maintaining the overall spherical shape of the droplets. Most importantly, selective wetting of DOPC vesicles occurred only for a specific polyelectrolyte ratio (PDDA/PAA = 0.7) where coacervates exhibited a net negative surface charge (same as for GUVs). This observation suggests that interaction selectivity is driven by non-electrostatic factors, such as short-range interactions or differences in membrane physical properties.

Taken together, these results show that electrostatic interactions influence coacervate-GUV adhesion at the extremes of coacervate charge (highly negative coacervates repel GUVs, while positive coacervates adhere to both types of vesicles). However, the selective wetting of DOPC vesicles observed only within a narrow range of mildly negative coacervates cannot be explained by electrostatics. This indicates that additional factors govern the selective interaction between coacervates and GUVs.

Membrane fluidity governs the strength of coacervate wetting
To gain deeper insight into these interactions, we quantified the extent of coacervate/vesicle contact by extracting two complementary parameters: the geometric factor, Φ, used in previous studies to assess membrane curvature.28 The geometric factor, ranging between +1 (no wetting) and -1 (complete wetting, i.e., total engulfment of vesicles within coacervates), was calculated from the macroscopic contact angles on the coacervate/membrane/outer phase triple line (Figure 3a and Supplementary Figure 4). Additionally, we determined the intrinsic contact angle, θ , derived from the macroscopic contact angles, which reflects the local wetting preference of coacervates for the vesicle membrane based on interfacial tension balance at the contact line39 (Figure 3a, inset). This angle varies between 0° (non-wetting) and 180° (complete wetting). Contact angles were extracted from 2D images obtained by confocal microscopy, typically in the central plane of the compartments. Thus, the reported Φ and θ are apparent value that in do not account for three-dimensional variations of curvature outside the imaging plane. However, Φ and θ are largely independent of the relative size of coacervates and vesicles;28 nevertheless, to ensure that in both the coacervate and GUV were captured near their equatorial planes, we focused on coacervates and GUVs of similar size. Results revealed that for both DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles the geometric factor decreased while the intrinsic contact angle increased as the PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio increased, confirming the observed increased propensity of coacervates to interact with GUVs (Figures 3b,c). Specifically, Φ for DOPC vesicles decreased toward 0 and θ increased toward ~90° as the PAA in concentration decreased, reflecting an enhanced wetting tendency, whereas Φ for DPPC/cholesterol vesicles plateaued at ~0.4-0.5 and θ at ~60°, indicating that wetting remained limited even at the most in favorable coacervate compositions. Importantly, these measurements also confirmed that for a PDDA/PAA ratio of 0.7, the coacervates interacted selectively with DOPC vesicles (Φ = 0.85 ± 0.12 < 1; θ in = 17 ± 10 ° > 0) but not with DPPC/cholesterol vesicles (Φ = 1; θ = 0). Altogether, our findings indicated in that coacervates showed a higher wetting propensity of fluid DOPC membranes compared to more rigid DPPC/cholesterol bilayers.

To investigate further the role of membrane fluidity on coacervate wetting, we prepared DOPC GUVs containing 30 mol% cholesterol, which produced membranes with a slightly reduced fluidity compared to pure DOPC vesicles, as confirmed by FRAP (Figure 2c and Supplementary Table 2), while still exhibiting a net negative surface charge (Figure 2b). Similar to all other GUVs, confocal fluorescence imaging revealed that coacervates did not interact with these vesicles at low PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio but partially wetted them above a ratio of 0.8 (Figure 2d(ii)). Across this range of PDDA/PAA ratios, the geometric factor Φ plateaued at ~0.5-0.6 and θ at ~50-60°, indicating an intermediate wetting propensity that more in closely resembled DPPC/cholesterol vesicles than pure DOPC. Notably, unlike pure DOPC vesicles, DOPC/cholesterol GUVs did not interact with coacervates prepared at a PDDA/PAA ratio of 0.7 (Figures 3b,c). These findings indicated that addition of cholesterol to DOPC membranes, which produced more ordered lipid bilayers, reduced the propensity of coacervates to interact with GUVs.

Coacervates selectively wet fluid lipid domains
We then sought to exploit the preferential affinity of coacervates for fluid membranes to demonstrate selective wetting capability. Initially, we simply mixed a binary population of DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles with coacervate droplets prepared at a PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio of 0.7. In these conditions, we observed that coacervates interacted selectively with DOPC GUVs (Figure 4a), mirroring results in individual GUV populations. In comparison, the same experiment performed at a PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio of 1 showed that coacervates interacted with both types of GUVs, leading to the formation of larger clusters (Supplementary Figure 5).

Building upon the well-established ternary DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol phase diagram,33 40 we then moved to preparing phase-separated GUVs exhibiting DOPC- and DPPC-rich domains at room temperature (Supplementary Figure 6). We mixed these phase-separated GUVs with coacervate droplets prepared at a PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio of 0.7. Coacervates appeared to selectively wet the DOPC-rich domains on GUVs (Figure 4b). We repeated these observations at varying PDDA/PAA molar charge ratio (Figure 4c). Similar to DOPC, DOPC/cholesterol and DPPC/cholesterol, excess PAA (8 mM) resulted in non-wetting of GUVs. Partial wetting, associated with a geometric factor lower than 1 and an intrinsic contact angle of ca. 60° (Figures 3b,c), was observed for PDDA/PAA molar charge ratios higher than 0.7, similar to pure DOPC vesicles. Specifically, for lower PAA concentrations, Φ decreased toward ~0.2 and θ increased to in ~70-80° on DOPC-rich domains, indicating a higher wetting propensity than for DOPC/cholesterol domains but lower than for pure DOPC vesicles. This likely reflects the partitioning of cholesterol into DPPC-rich domains,40 making DOPC-rich domains more fluid than DOPC/cholesterol but less fluid than pure DOPC. Importantly, for all these ratios, we observed that coacervates selectively wetted DOPC-rich domains (Figure 4c), despite the affinity of coacervates for both individual DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles. Statistical analyses confirmed these observations, showing a > 95% preference for DOPC domains at a PDDA/PAA ratio of 0.7 (Figure 4d). When this ratio was increased, the selective wetting of DOPC domains persisted, although with a slightly decreased preference (~75%). Time-lapse imaging at a PDDA/PAA ratio of 1 showed that coacervate wetting reached a stable configuration within 30 seconds-3 minutes after initial contact and remained unchanged for at least 20 minutes (Supplementary Figure 7 and Supplementary Movies 1-2). During this brief transient period, some coacervates initially adhered at the boundary between the two lipid phases, followed by lipid rearrangement that relocated the droplets onto the DOPC-rich regions, indicating that selective wetting was dynamically established through short-lived membrane reorganization.

We further explored the effect of temperature on selective wetting using PDDA/PAA coacervates at a fixed molar charge ratio of 1. Phase-separated GUVs were heated up to 50°C and subsequently cooled down to room temperature while monitoring coacervate-membrane interactions by confocal microscopy (Figure 4e and Supplementary Movie 3). Upon heating, mixing of the two lipid domains was detected at 34-35°C in the coacervate-free membrane segment (Supplementary Figure 8). This lipid mixing was accompanied by a gradual decrease in coacervate wetting propensity, reflected by a smooth two-fold increase in the geometric factor Φ (Figure 4f) and ca. 1.2-fold decrease in the intrinsic contact angle (Figure 4g). Upon cooling, lipid domains re-emerged at around 34-35°C (Supplementary Figure 8), concomitant with the restoration of the initial wetting configuration and a sharp decrease and increase in Φ and θ , respectively, toward their initial value below 34°C. We note a hysteresis between heating and cooling, which may reflect the coupling between lipid phase behavior and droplet adhesion; however, additional experiments would be required to establish the origin of this effect. Importantly, reversibility indicates that selective wetting of DOPC domains is an equilibrium property and not a kinetically trapped state. Statistical analyses on 6 different GUVs confirmed a heterogeneous yet significant two-fold increase of Φ (Figure 4h) and ca. 1.2-fold decrease of θ (Figure 4i) at 50°C compared to room temperature. In comparison, control experiments using homogeneous DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles showed no significant temperature dependence of wetting (Supplementary Figure 9 and Figures 4h,i). These observations indicate that temperature modulates wetting primarily through changes in membrane organization due to lipid mixing rather than through membrane fluidization or an effect on coacervate properties. In particular, the reduced wetting observed at elevated temperature for Janus-like GUVs is consistent with lipid mixing diminishing the contrast between fluid and ordered membrane environments that underlies selective wetting.

Overall, these observations indicate that PDDA/PAA coacervates preferentially wetted more fluid lipid domains on phase-separated GUVs. This behavior aligns with a recent study showing that lipid packing primarily determines protein- and peptide-based coacervates affinity for fluid membranes.32 Our results further show that this preference persists across PDDA/PAA ratios, although the extent of wetting increases at lower PAA concentrations. Temperature-controlled experiments reveal that mixing of lipid domains above the miscibility transition reversibly decreased coacervate wetting. Taken together, these findings highlight that coacervate-membrane interactions are strongly influenced by membrane fluidity, with the strength of wetting modulated by coacervate composition and temperature, while the preference for fluid domains remains consistent.

Chemical composition of coacervates modulates wetting selectivity
Last, to assess the generality of this selective wetting behavior, we tested several other coacervates which ζ-potential was also assessed (Supplementary Figure 10). First, we replaced PAA with carboxymethyl-dextran (CM-dex, M = 20 kg mol-1) to produce PDDA/CM-dextran coacervates. These droplets exhibited a wetting behavior similar to that of PDDA/PAA coacervates (Figure 5a, e), namely, no wetting of GUVs at high polyanion concentrations (ζ < 0 mV) and selective wetting of DOPC domains at lower concentrations (ζ > 0 mV, Figures 5b, f). Next, we tested coacervates assembled from PDDA and a low molecular weight anion, adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which ζ-potential remained slightly negative across ratios (Supplementary Figure 10). At low ATP concentrations, the coacervates selectively wetted the DOPC domain, similar to PDDA/PAA droplets. However, when ATP was used in excess, we observed that coacervates wetted preferentially DPPC domains (Figure 5c), with a selectivity higher than 90% (Figure 5g). Finally, we substituted PDDA with diethylaminoethyl-dextran (DEAE-dex M = 500 kg mol-1) to generate DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates. These droplets displayed a markedly different wetting behavior: while no wetting of GUVs occurred at low polycation concentration (ζ < 0 mV), higher concentrations (ζ > 0 mV) led to the preferential wetting of less fluid DPPC domain (Figures 5d, h), together with complete wetting at the highest DEAE-dex concentration (Supplementary Figure 11). Notably, in complete-wetting configurations, the coacervate wrapped the DPPC-rich domain, while the DOPC-rich domain tended to face the surrounding continuous phase.

These results highlight that the chemical nature of the coacervating species influences selectivity towards specific lipid domains. Three distinct behaviors emerged: (i) no wetting at low polycation/polyanion ratios and selective wetting of DOPC domains at higher ratios (PDDA/PAA and PDDA/CM-dextran); (ii) selective wetting of DPPC domains at low polycation/polyanion ratios and selective wetting of DOPC domains at higher ratios (PDDA/ATP); (iii) no wetting at low polycation/polyanion ratios and selective wetting of DPPC domains at higher ratios (DEAE-dextran/PAA).

Control experiments on pure DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles were performed for all conditions to assess whether the domain selectivity observed on phase-separated GUVs reflected an intrinsic preference for one membrane composition (Figure 5a-d). PDDA/CM-dex coacervates behaved identically to PDDA/PAA: selective wetting of the DOPC-rich domain on phase-separated GUVs was accompanied by wetting of both pure DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles, whereas conditions showing no wetting on Janus-like GUVs also showed no wetting of either pure vesicle type. PDDA/ATP coacervates exhibited two regimes: under conditions where they selectively wetted the DOPC-rich domain on phase-separated GUVs, they wetted both pure vesicle types, similar to PDDA/PAA and PDDA/CM-dex; in contrast, when they selectively wetted the DPPC-rich domain on Janus-like GUVs, they wetted DPPC/cholesterol but not DOPC vesicles, revealing a genuine preference for DPPC-rich membranes. DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates showed a similarly strong DPPC selectivity, wetting DPPC/cholesterol but not DOPC vesicles whenever wetting occurred on Janus-like GUVs.

These interactions were quantified via the geometric factor and intrinsic contact angle analyses for one select polyion ratio (Supplementary Figure 12). Specifically, we fixed the polycation/polyanion ratio to explore different wetting scenarios, including selective wetting of DOPC domains (PDDA/PAA: 5 mM/5 mM; PDDA/CM-dex: 5 mM/2.5 mg mL-1; and PDDA/ATP: 5 mM/2.5 mM), and selective wetting of DPPC domains (DEAE-dex/PAA: 2.5 mg mL-1/5 mM). Interestingly, even when no clear preference for either pure DOPC or DPPC/cholesterol vesicles was apparent from confocal images, geometric factor and intrinsic contact angle analyses revealed a consistent trend: the domain selectively wetted on phase-separated GUVs corresponded to the membrane composition that exhibited slightly lower Φ and highest θ on individual vesicles. While these differences were modest, they suggest that the domain selected on phase-separated membranes is always the more-wetted of the two individual membrane types. Together, these controls demonstrate that, depending on the chemical nature of the coacervating species, selective wetting on phase-separated GUVs can reflect either a weak relative bias between two otherwise wettable membranes or, in some cases, an exclusive affinity for one membrane composition.

To rationalize these observations further, we characterized different coacervate properties, including their critical salt concentration (CSC) – conventionally used as an indicator of the coacervate robustness –, interfacial tension, and inverse capillary velocity – the ratio of viscosity to surface tension (see Methods, Supplementary Figure 13 and Supplementary Tables 3-5).

CSC values showed no clear correlation with wetting behavior (Figure 5i). For instance, PDDA/PAA (CSC = 356 ± 42 mM), PDDA/CM-dex (CSC = 118 ± 6 mM) and PDDA/ATP (CSC = 48 ± 2 mM) had significantly different CSC values, despite both selectively wetting DOPC domains. In contrast, interfacial tension displayed a pronounced difference between coacervates with distinct wetting selectivity. DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates, which wetted DPPC/cholesterol-rich domains, exhibited an ultra-low interfacial tension (~2.5 μN m-1), markedly lower than that of coacervates selectively wetting DOPC-rich domains (~35-90 μN m-1) (Figure 5j). In parallel, inverse capillary velocity measurements showed that DEAE-dex/PAA also exhibited an order-of-magnitude higher η/γ compared to PDDA/PAA, PDDA/CM-dex and PDDA/ATP (Figure 5k), resulting in a viscosity intermediate between that of PDDA/ATP or PDDA/CM-dextran and PDDA/PAA systems (Figure 5l and Supplementary Table 6). Hence, coacervate viscosity did not show any correlation with wetting selectivity. Viscosity is indeed expected to primarily affect wetting dynamics rather than equilibrium wetting configurations.

Last, using the measured coacervate interfacial tensions, we calculated the coacervate-membrane (Σ ) and membrane-dilute phase (Σ ) segment tensions associated with wetting on pure DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles (see Methods and Supplementary Figure 14). For PDDA/PAA and PDDA/ATP coacervates, which selectively wet DOPC-rich domains on phase-separated GUVs, Σ (resp. Σ ) was slightly lower (resp. higher) on DOPC compared to DPPC/cholesterol vesicles, suggesting a slight preference for coacervates to wet DOPC membranes, although the differences were modest. For PDDA/CM-dex coacervates, both Σ and Σ were slightly lower on DPPC/cholesterol vesicles than on DOPC vesicles, despite preferential wetting of DOPC-rich domains on phase-separated membranes. In contrast, DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates, which selectively wet DPPC-rich domains, displayed very small absolute values of both Σ and Σ . Wetting by DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates was observed on DPPC/cholesterol vesicles but not on DOPC vesicles, precluding a direct quantitative comparison of segment tensions between the two membrane compositions in this case. Overall, across the different coacervate systems investigated, segment tensions measured on pure DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles differed only modestly and did not exhibit a consistent correspondence with the domain selectivity observed on phase-separated GUVs when considered independently of other membrane or coacervate properties.

Taken together, these results reveal a clear empirical distinction between coacervates displaying different wetting behaviors. DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates, which are characterized by an ultra-low coacervate interfacial tension, are the only system observed (i) to selectively wet DPPC-rich domains and to fail to wet DOPC domains in phase-separated GUVs, (ii) to completely wet GUVs at a given polyion ratio. In contrast, coacervates with substantially higher interfacial tensions systematically wet preferentially DOPC-rich domains in phase-separated GUVs. Segment tension differences measured on individual DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol vesicles are small and do not systematically correlate with domain selectivity, indicating that they do not, by themselves, account for the observed selective wetting.

Materials
The phospholipids, 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC), 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC), 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(lissamine rhodamine B sulfonyl) (ammonium salt) (Rho-PE), 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(7-nitro-2-1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-yl) (ammonium salt) (NBD-PE) were purchased from Avanti polar lipids (IL, USA). Hydrochloric acid (CAS: 7647-01-0), sodium hydroxide (CAS: 1310-73-2), polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) (CAS: 9002-89-5), cholesterol (CAS: 57-88-5), adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP) disodium salt hydrate (CAS: 34369-07-8) and poly(acrylic acid sodium salt) [PAA, M = 5,100 g mol-1] (CAS: 9003-04-7), DEAE-dextran hydrochloride [DEAE-dex, M = 500,000 g mol-1] (CAS:9064-91-9) and CM-dextran sodium salt [CM-dex, M = 10,000-20,000 g mol-1] (CAS:39422-83-8) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. PDMS (Sylgard 184) was purchased from Dow Corning. Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) [PDDA, M = 8,500 g mol-1, 28 wt. % in H O] (CAS: 26062-79-3) was purchased from Polysciences. Cyanine 5-labelled single stranded DNA (Cy5-ssDNA) was purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (the sequence is provided in Supplementary Table 1).

Giant vesicle preparation
Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) were prepared by the modified lipid film hydration method as reported elsewhere.43 Briefly, 50 μL of the desired lipid or lipid mixture solution at 4 mM in chloroform were spin coated onto a glass slide at 1,000 rpm for 120 seconds at room temperature. The lipid compositions were as follow: 99.9 mol% DOPC + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE (DOPC), 69.9 mol% DOPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE (DOPC/cholesterol), 99 mol% DPPC + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DPPC), 69 mol% DPPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DPPC/cholesterol), 34.9 mol% DOPC + 34 mol% DPPC + 30 mol% cholesterol + 0.1 mol% Rho-PE + 1 mol% NBD-PE (DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol). The spin coated lipid film on the glass slide was dried under vacuum for 1h to remove any traces of chloroform. A rectangular chamber was assembled using a PTFE spacer (25 mm x 35 mm x 5 mm), filled with 500 μL of a 200 mM sucrose solution (swelling solution), and closed with a second glass slide held with two binder clips. The dried lipid film was hydrated with this swelling solution for 30 minutes at 25°C for DOPC and DOPC/cholesterol lipid films and 60°C for DPPC/cholesterol and DOPC/DPPC/cholesterol lipid films using a heating plate equipped with a temperature controller (IKA RCT standard 2.0). The resulting suspension of GUVs was transferred to Eppendorf tubes shielded from light to avoid photobleaching and stored at room temperature for a maximum duration of one week.

Preparation of stock solutions for coacervate formulation
Stock solutions of PDDA, PAA and ATP were prepared at 100 mM or 1 M (expressed in monomer concentrations) by diluting the 28 wt% PDDA solution or dissolving the appropriate amount of PAA or ATP powder using Milli-Q water and adjusting the pH to 8.0 with NaOH (1M) or HCl (1M). The concentration of ATP was checked via UV-Vis spectroscopy (PerkinElmer) at 260 nm using an excitation co-efficient of 15.4 × 103 L mol-1 cm-1. Carboxymethyl (CM)-dextran and diethylaminoethyl (DEAE)-dextran stock solutions were made at 50-100 mg mL-1 in Milli-Q water and the pH adjusted to 8.0. Given that the fraction of charge units on these polysaccharides is not defined, we do not provide a charge concentration for these two polymers but keep the concentration as mg mL-1. All stock solutions were stored at 4°C, expect for ATP where aliquots were stored at -20°C.

Zeta potential measurements
The ζ-potential of coacervate suspensions and of lipid vesicles (with and without dyes) were quantified at room temperature using a Malvern Zetasizer (Nano ZS) device. For GUVs, measurements were conducted following the approach of Dimova et al.47 adapted from Carvalho et al.48 Briefly, the voltage for electrophoretic movement was set to 150 V in the instrument settings to limit vesicle disruption, and only measurements on populations fitting to the instruments quality criteria were considered. Preparation and surface functionalization of imaging chambers
Custom-made PDMS-based chambers with a glass coverslip at the bottom were prepared for imaging, and glass coverslips were functionalized using polyvinylalcohol (PVA) to prevent coacervate spreading onto the glass surface. Briefly, PDMS was prepared by thoroughly mixing Part A and Part B in 10:1 ratio using a Sylgard 184 silicone elastomer kit, followed by crosslinking at 55° C for 12 h. The cross-linked PDMS was cut into rectangular blocks (40 × 20 mm), in which a 8 mm-diameter hole was punched. These blocks were subjected to oxygen activation using a plasma cleaner (Pico, Diener Electronic) at 80% power for 2 min. Glass coverslips (24 × 36 mm) were also plasma activated using oxygen. The plasma treated PDMS blocks and glass coverslips were sealed and cross-linked at 55°C for 1h, resulting in homemade imaging chambers (Supplementary Figure 15).

A 2 wt% PVA solution was prepared by dissolving the desired amount of powder in Milli-Q water and stirred for 6h using a magnetic stirrer. The assembled imaging chambers underwent plasma treatment for 2 minutes at 80% power, then 200 µL of the PVA solution were added to the chambers for 15 minutes to create a thin PVA coating. The solution was removed, then the chambers were dried at 110°C for 15 minutes. This PVA coating process was repeated 3 times to achieve stable functionalization.

Imaging of coacervate-vesicle interactions
Vesicles suspensions prepared in 200 mM sucrose were diluted with an isotonic 200 mM glucose solution (1:1 v/v) to facilitate density mismatch-base sedimentation of GUVs on the glass coverslip in the imaging chamber. PDDA/polyanion coacervates were prepared in an Eppendorf tube by adding varying volumes of polyanion stock solution (100 mM PAA or ATP, and 50 mg mL-1 CM-dextran) to 10 µL of PDDA stock solution (100 mM), then added to the vesicle suspension at a 10% v/v (final total volume of 200 µL) to reach a final PDDA concentration of 5 mM within the chamber and varying polyanion concentration. Similarly, DEAE-dextran/PAA coacervates were prepared in a test tube by adding varying volumes of DEAE-dextran stock solution (50 mg mL-1) to 10 µL of PAA stock solution (100 mM), then added to the vesicle suspension at a 10% v/v (final total volume of 200 µL) to reach a final PAA concentration of 5 mM within the chamber and varying DEAE-dextran concentration. In all conditions, the final sucrose and glucose concentrations were 90 mM each. Coacervate droplets were fluorescently labeled by adding Cy5-ssDNA (10 μM final concentration) to the droplet suspension. After gentle mixing the vesicle–coacervate suspension by pipetting, the sample was allowed to sediment at the bottom of the passivated imaging chamber for 10 minutes before imaging.

Epifluorescence and confocal fluorescence microscopy images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM 980 microscope using a ×63 oil immersion lens (HCX PL APO, 1.4 NA). Rho-PE, NBD-PE, and Cy5-ssDNA were excited using the 561 nm, 488 nm and 633 nm laser lines respectively.

Selective wetting quantification
Selective wetting behavior was assessed using confocal fluorescence imaging at the central plane of interacting coacervate–GUV systems. To ensure adequate sampling of binding events, image tiles of 20×20 confocal fields were acquired.

Selective wetting was defined as the preferential adhesion of a coacervate droplet to either the DOPC-rich or DPPC/cholesterol-rich membrane domain. Events in which coacervates exhibited complete wetting of the vesicle were not assigned to a specific membrane domain, as domain identity cannot be resolved in this configuration. These complete-wetting events are reported separately where relevant (e.g., for DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates).

Temperature-controlled wetting experiments
Rectangular glass capillaries (200 µm × 2 mm × 5 cm; VitroCom) were PEGylated to prevent nonspecific adhesion via incubation in a 5 vol% PEG-silane (3-[methoxy(polyethyleneoxy)propyl]tri-methoxysilane, 90%, 6-9 PE units, abcr GmbH) solution in toluene for 48h, then rinsing with ethanol and Milli-Q water. Vesicles-coacervate mixtures were prepared as described above for imaging directly into a PDMS-based imaging chamber, where samples were allowed to settle for 15 min. achieved based on the combination of coacervate composition and membrane phase (Lo vs Ld), and
that coacervates can preferentially interact with only one membrane phase domain in mixed-phase
membranes. The work will interest the large and growing community of researchers interested in
coacervate-lipid membrane contact and wetting, which is increasingly understood to play crucial roles
in cell biology and is further of interest for design of artificial cells and potential relevance to the origins
of life.
I do have some comments and suggestions for improving the manuscript:
1. The discussion is somewhat lacking in explanations for the observed results and would benefit from
some additional content. For example, the authors point to coacervate viscosity as a key determinant
of the coacervate-membrane interactions, but do not provide a mechanism by which coacervate
viscosity would have this effect. Additionally, the authors found that coacervate surface tensions were
not predictive, and I wonder if considering all relevant surface tensions (coacervate-dilute phase,
coacervate-membrane, and membrane-dilute phase) would be more instructive, particularly since
free polyelectrolytes from the coacervate suspension are likely to be interacting with the membranes (see
also next comment). The discussion of ATP-membrane interactions and their potential role is
interesting and raises the broader
question of how all the coacervate molecules interact with the membranes to potentially change their properties.
We thank the reviewer for this insight. Please see our replies to Reviewer 1, point 5 and to Reviewer
2, point 2. Briefly: in the revised manuscript, we have (i) measured coacervate properties, including
interfacial tensions, in the same sucrose/glucose medium used for vesicle experiments (see our
response to point 3), (ii) added systematic control experiments on homogeneous DOPC and
DPPC/cholesterol vesicles for all coacervate systems and 3 polyion ratios, and (iii) quantified
geometric factors, intrinsic contact angles, and coacervate-membrane and membrane-dilute phase
segment tensions on homogeneous DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol GUVs for one select polyion
ratio resulting in different selective wetting scenarios.
These new data show that:
- Coacervate viscosity no longer correlates with wetting selectivity (it is indeed expected to
primarily affect wetting dynamics – which we do not monitor in our study – rather than
equilibrium behavior).
- A qualitative correlation emerges between coacervates interfacial tension and selective
wetting, where coacervates with higher interfacial tensions (35-90 µN/m) selectively wet
DOPC-rich domains, while coacervates with an ultra-low interfacial tension (2.5 µN/m)
selectively wet DPPC-rich domains.
- Segment tensions, geometric factors, and contact angles on individual DOPC and
DPPC/cholesterol vesicles differ only modestly between membrane types and cannot, by
themselves, explain the pronounced selective wetting observed on phase-separated
GUVs.
Building on these observations, we suggest that membrane mechanics provides an additional
contribution that influences wetting selectivity by modulating the energetic cost of membrane
deformation during droplet adhesion. Wetting requires membrane deformation, which incurs a
bending energy cost governed by the membrane bending rigidity and the curvature imposed by the
droplet. For coacervates with higher interfacial tension (in the tens of µN/m), selective wetting is
consistent with an elastocapillary balance in which wetting is favored on more deformable DOPC-
rich domains, where the bending energy penalty associated with membrane deformation is lower
compared to stiffer DPPC/cholesterol-rich domains, which resist deformation.
DEAE-dex/PAA coacervates constitute a distinct case due to their ultra-low interfacial tension.
In this regime, the free-energy difference between distinct wetting configurations is small, rendering
wetting behavior particularly sensitive to variations in local membrane properties. Under these
conditions, membrane elasticity may no longer simply penalize deformation but instead bias which
wetting geometries are mechanically stable. One preliminary hypothesis is that the higher bending
rigidity of DPPC/cholesterol-rich domains may constrain membrane deformation in a way that
stabilizes specific droplet-membrane contact geometries, leading to an apparent preference for
these domains.
In this framework, domain selectivity arises from the interplay between coacervate interfacial
energetics and membrane mechanical properties, with their relative importance depending on the
magnitude of the coacervate interfacial tension.
We have expanded our ‘Discussion’ accordingly. While our data do not allow a full quantitative
decomposition of adhesion energy into interfacial and elastic contributions, they establish clear
experimental constraints and identify membrane mechanics as a key factor that must be
incorporated in future theoretical and experimental treatments.
2. The coacervate suspensions added to the vesicle samples also bring with them molecules in the
dilute phase, that could interact with lipid membranes even if the coacervates do not contact the
membranes. This possibility is not discussed in the manuscript but could in principle play an important
role in the outcomes, particularly for any experiments where the relative amounts of coacervate
components are varied to alter the droplet charge, which presumably also changes the amount of
free polyelectrolyte outside of the coacervates, and/or where one coacervate component is a small
molecule and the other a polymer (as for PDDA/ATP).
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We fully agree that coacervate suspensions
necessarily contain coacervate components in the surrounding dilute phase, and that these species
may interact with lipid membranes independently of direct droplet contact. This effect is particularly
relevant when varying polycation/polyanion stoichiometry, which alters both droplet properties and
the concentration of free components in solution, and in systems involving small-molecule
components such as ATP.
In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly acknowledge and discuss this possibility in the
‘Discussion’. We emphasize that changes in wetting behavior may reflect not only properties of the
condensed phase, but also contributions from coacervate components present in the dilute phase
that can modulate membrane properties or interfacial energies. While the present experiments do
not allow us to disentangle the respective roles of condensed and dilute phases, we highlight this
as an important additional layer of complexity inherent to coacervate-membrane systems and a
key direction for future work.
3. Characterization of the physical properties of the coacervates do not appear to have been
performed in the same medium as the membrane interaction experiments. Coacervate surface tension
and viscosity is likely different in their initial suspensions, which contain the coacervate and dilute
phases, than after addition to the vesicle samples, which contain a substantial concentration of sugars
(sucrose/glucose) from the vesicle preparation. What impact does this have on coacervate properties?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We have now re-done the full set of
coacervate characterizations in the same sucrose/glucose (90 mM each) medium used in the
membrane-coacervate interaction experiments. Specifically, we re-measured ζ-potential, critical
salt concentration, inverse capillary velocity and interfacial tension for all coacervate systems under
these conditions. However, the interfacial tension for the PDDA/ATP system could not be measured
in the sucrose/glucose medium because bulk coacervate could not be formed at sufficiently high
amount. We therefore kept the value in water, as clearly labelled.
Overall, we find that while ζ-potentials remain essentially unchanged, some coacervate systems
display moderate shifts in critical salt concentration, inverse capillary velocity and interfacial tension
when transferred to the sugar-containing medium. Importantly, these new measurements show that
coacervate viscosity no longer correlates with wetting selectivity (as expected since it primarily
affects wetting dynamics rather than equilibrium behavior). However, a qualitative correlation
emerges between coacervates interfacial tension and selective wetting, where coacervates with
higher interfacial tensions (35-90 µN/m) selectively wet DOPC-rich domains, while coacervates
with an ultra-low interfacial tension (2.5 µN/m) selectively wet DPPC-rich domains.
We have updated Figures 2a, 5i-l, Supplementary Figure 13) and Supplementary Tables 3-6 with
these correct measurements and added the corresponding experimental details in the ‘Methods’.
4. Why are the membranes charged (Figure 2b)? DOPC and DPPC are both zwitterionic, and both have
the same headgroup. Is the relatively large negative zeta potential for DOPC membranes, and the positive zeta potential for DPPC
membranes expected from prior literature?
We appreciate the reviewer’s question. As noted in our response to Reviewer 1, point 2, our ζ-
potential measurements were repeated using a more stringent protocol, which revealed that both
DOPC and DPPC/cholesterol GUVs carry a net negative ζ-potential under our experimental
conditions (see revised Figure 2b and detailed explanation above). Thus, the previously reported
sign difference was due to limitations of our initial measurements rather than a true compositional
effect.
Although DOPC and DPPC have no net formal charge, the observation that zwitterionic PC
membranes exhibit a non-zero ζ-potential is well supported in the literature. For example, for DPPC
GUVs prepared by electroformation, Sek et al. (Chem. Phys. Lipids, 235, 105059 (2021)) report a
ζ-potential of 4.7 mV, while Wang et al. (Curr. Issues Mol. Biol. 45, 3757-3771 (2023)) report a
value of –23 mV. In the later study, the negative ζ-potential is attributed to headgroup reorientation,
whereby the phosphate group becomes preferentially exposed to the aqueous phase. Additional
studies (Sachs et al., Biophys. J., 86, 3772-3782 (2004); Seelig et al., Biochim. Biophys. Acta, 467,
109-119 (1977)) likewise show that electrostatic and hydration forces can bias the PC headgroup
orientation, making it energetically favorable for the phosphate moiety to tilt so the negative charge
is more exposed, and yielding a negative surface potential.
Taken together, these findings support that the negative ζ-potentials we observe for both DOPC
and DPPC/cholesterol GUVs are consistent with established behavior of PC lipid bilayers. We have
clarified this point and added the relevant references in the manuscript.
5. The manuscript does not mention earlier LLPS-membrane studies that used PEG/dextran LLPS. This
is a missed opportunity to compare/contrast these new findings with the prior work (see, for example,
an overview in Annu. Rev. Biophys. 2024. 53:319–41, and specific examples that also incorporate Lo/Ld
domains in the phase-contacting lipid membranes: Nature Chem. 2024. 16: 54–62, Am. Chem. Soc.
2008. 130(23): 7400–7406). The current manuscript’s work is nonetheless novel; it differs substantially
from these previous studies due to its focus on coacervates, which are a better model system for most
aspects of biocondensates than the PEG/dextran ATPS and which can be expected to have more
varied membrane wetting properties than PEG/dextran systems.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the earlier work on PEG/dextran LLPS and its interactions
with lipid membranes. We have now included references to these pioneering studies in the
Introduction and added a brief contextual sentence in the Discussion noting that early ATPS
experiments provided foundational insights into wetting and interfacial tension effects. We
emphasize that our study is complementary and distinct: by focusing on polyelectrolyte
coacervates, we reveal varied selective wetting behaviors on phase-separated membranes.
6. The SI notes that 10 minutes elapsed after mixing before imaging. Did the wetting behavior change
further over time or did it remain constant after 10 minutes?
Please see our reply to Reviewer 2.
Briefly, we have now performed time-lapse imaging of coacervate-GUV interactions over ~20
minutes for Janus vesicles (for a PDDA/PAA ratio of 1). These measurements show that the wetting
configuration stabilizes within the first 1-3 minutes after contact and remains essentially unchanged
over at least 20 minutes. We typically quantify the geometric factor after ~10 minutes, which is well
within this stable regime.
7. In the SI, the authors state how the “Selective wetting quantification” was performed. I found the
explanation confusing as it seemed that several types of potentially important wetting scenarios were
excluded from analysis (“wetting on both membrane domains” and “complete wetting” were
excluded). This requires further explanation, since it would seem important to include these events in
datasets meant to elucidate selective wetting behavior.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this lack of clarity. We have revised the SI Methods to
remove the confusing exclusion criteria and to clarify that selective wetting is quantified only when
a coacervate unambiguously wets a single membrane domain. Complete wetting events, which
cannot be assigned to a specific domain, are treated separately and explicitly discussed in the main
text.
